questions.q: What is the practical difference between `dependencies` and `devDependencies` in package.json?
options: dependencies are needed for the program to run (e.g. ethers); devDependencies are only needed while building/developing (e.g. the TypeScript compiler), and can be skipped in production with --omit=dev
There is no real difference — npm treats them identically
devDependencies are always installed globally, dependencies are always local
dependencies can only be npm's own built-in packages
questions.explain: dependencies ship with the running program; devDependencies (like typescript or tsx) are only needed to build or develop it, and a production install can skip them with --omit=dev.

questions.q: Given `"ethers": "^6.13.0"` in package.json, which of these versions could `npm install` legally resolve to?
questions.explain: A caret (^) range allows any minor or patch update within the same major version — so 6.13.0 up to (but not including) 7.0.0, which includes 6.15.2 — but not a different major version like 7.0.0 or 5.9.0.

questions.q: What does package-lock.json record that package.json does not?
options: Nothing — the two files contain the same information
Only the devDependencies, never the dependencies
The exact resolved version of every package in the whole dependency tree, including sub-dependencies you never listed yourself
questions.explain: package.json specifies allowed ranges (like ^6.13.0); package-lock.json pins the exact version that was actually installed for every package, including transitive dependencies, making installs reproducible.

questions.q: What does running `npx tsx src/index.ts` do differently from a plain global install of tsx?
options: It runs tsx's CLI on demand, downloading it temporarily if it isn't already installed, without requiring a permanent global install
It installs tsx permanently and globally, identical to `npm install -g tsx`
It only works if the project has no package.json
questions.explain: npx runs a package's command-line tool on demand — using it locally if present, or fetching it temporarily if not — avoiding the need to clutter a global install for a tool you only use occasionally.

questions.q: Why should a deployment pipeline typically run `npm install --omit=dev` rather than a plain `npm install`?
options: Because --omit=dev installs packages faster regardless of what's being deployed
Because production doesn't need build-time-only tools like the TypeScript compiler, only what the already-built program needs to run
Because devDependencies contain secrets that must never be installed anywhere
Because --omit=dev is required to make bigint literals work
questions.explain: devDependencies like typescript or tsx are only needed to build/develop the project — a production server running the already-compiled JavaScript has no need to ship a compiler alongside it.
